items.content_html:
In github.com/insomniacslk/dhcp/dhcpv4/nclient4, BroadcastRawUDPConn.ReadFrom does not validate that the IPv4 payload length is sufficient to hold a UDP header before calculating the DHCP payload length. A frame with an IPv4 total-length field specifying fewer than eight payload bytes results in a negative DHCP length, causing a panic in buf.Consume due to a negative slice bound.

References

  • https://github.com/insomniacslk/dhcp/pull/583
  • https://github.com/insomniacslk/dhcp/commit/c76316d4aa825673b208730779843d0711021e81
  • https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6237
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jp3c-6v3g-mpxv

items.content_html:
Impact

What kind of vulnerability is it? Who is impacted?

When etcd is configured with --listen-client-http-urls to split the HTTP and gRPC client endpoints onto separate listeners, the --client-crl-file Certificate Revocation List is not enforced on the gRPC listener. A client presenting a revoked certificate is correctly rejected by the HTTP endpoint but continues to authenticate successfully over gRPC.

Patches

Has the problem been patched? What versions should users upgrade to?

This vulnerability is patched in the following versions:

  • etcd 3.6.13
  • etcd 3.5.32

Workarounds

Is there a way for users to fix or remediate the vulnerability without upgrading?

If upgrading is not immediately possible, reduce exposure by restricting network access to etcd client ports using firewall rules or network policy so that only trusted components can reach the server. This limits the pool of clients that could exploit a revoked certificate but does not enforce CRL revocation.

Reporter

Luis Toro (@lobuhi on Github)

items.content_html:
Summary

When validating an incoming block header, HeaderSigVerifier.verifyConsensusSize counts every set bit in PubKeysBitmap — including bits that correspond to no validator (the padding bits of the final byte, which exist whenever the consensus group size is not a multiple of 8). The subsequent BLS aggregate-signature verification (blsMultiSigner.Verify) only checks signature validity for real validator indices and silently ignores those padding bits. As a result, a malicious or compromised block producer can set the padding bits to make the on-bits reach the PBFT quorum while only gathering a smaller number of real validator signature shares, causing a block to be accepted as correctly signed without a genuine two-thirds validator quorum.

Details

Quorum counter counts padding bits — core/process/headerCheck/headerSignatureVerify.go:145-183:

func (hsv *HeaderSigVerifier) verifyConsensusSize(consensusPubKeys []string, header data.HeaderHandler) error {
    consensusSize := len(consensusPubKeys)
    bitmap := header.GetPubKeysBitmap()

    expectedBitmapSize := consensusSize / 8
    if consensusSize%8 != 0 {
        expectedBitmapSize++
    }
    if len(bitmap) != expectedBitmapSize {
        ...
        return ErrWrongSizeBitmap
    }

    numOfOnesInBitmap := 0
    for index := range bitmap {
        numOfOnesInBitmap += bits.OnesCount8(bitmap[index])   // <-- counts ALL bits incl. padding
    }

    minNumRequiredSignatures := consensus.GetPBFTThreshold(consensusSize)
    ...
    if numOfOnesInBitmap >= minNumRequiredSignatures {
        return nil
    }
    ...
    return ErrNotEnoughSignatures
}

The bitmap-byte-length check above only ensures the byte array is the right size; it never requires the padding bits (bits [consensusSize … expectedBitmapSize*8)) to be zero. So any combination of padding bits is accepted toward the quorum.

VerifySignature (:92-143) then builds the verifier from the real public keys, sets the aggregate signature, and calls verifier.Verify(hash, bitmap).

The BLS verifier ignores padding bits — crypto/signing/multisig/blsMultisig.go:272-297:

func (bms *blsMultiSigner) Verify(message []byte, bitmap []byte) error {
    ...
    maxFlags := len(bitmap) * 8
    flagsMismatch := maxFlags < len(bms.data.pubKeys)   // only rejects *too few* bytes
    if flagsMismatch {
        return crypto.ErrBitmapMismatch
    }

    pubKeys := make([]crypto.PublicKey, 0)
    for i := range bms.data.pubKeys {                    // <-- only real validator indices
        err := bms.isIndexInBitmap(uint16(i), bitmap)
        if err != nil {
            continue
        }
        pubKeys = append(pubKeys, bms.data.pubKeys[i])
    }

    return bms.llSigner.VerifyAggregatedSig(bms.keyGen.Suite(), pubKeys, bms.data.aggSig, message)
}

Because the loop only walks range bms.data.pubKeys, a bit set at position i >= len(pubKeys) is never inspected by isIndexInBitmap and is therefore silently dropped from signature verification, even though verifyConsensusSize already counted it toward quorum.

PBFT threshold — core/consensus/consensus.go:5-8 (consensusSize*2/3 + 1) and fallback :10-13 (consensusSize/2 + 1).

Reachable from received blocks — core/process/block/interceptedBlocks/interceptedBlock.go:181-201 runs CheckValidity() → VerifySignature on every header received from peers.

Worked example (consensus size = 5)

  • Required PBFT quorum: 5*2/3 + 1 = 4.
  • Valid validator bit positions: 0..4. Bits 5, 6, 7 are padding (no validator).
  • Attacker gathers only one real signature share (validator 0) and aggregates it.
  • Sets bitmap byte to 0b1110_0001 (0xE1): bit 0 (real) + bits 5, 6, 7 (padding).
  • verifyConsensusSize sees bits.OnesCount8(0xE1) = 4 ≥ 4 → passes quorum.
  • blsMultiSigner.Verify only validates against validator 0's public key (padding ignored) → passes.
  • The block is accepted with one real signer instead of four.

For any consensusSize not divisible by 8, up to 8 - (consensusSize % 8) fake "padding" signatures can be counted toward quorum. On a 21-member group (one padding bit) the attacker shaves one vote; on smaller/sharded groups with consensusSize % 8 close to 7 the relative impact is larger.

PoC

Reproduced locally against current develop (085a5d1) with this test (run under core/process/headerCheck, removed after verification):

func TestPOCHeaderSigVerifierCountsPaddingBitsTowardQuorum(t *testing.T) {
    args := createHeaderSigVerifierArgs()
    args.NodesCoordinator = &cMock.NodesCoordinatorMock{
        GetValidatorsPublicKeysCalled: func(_ []byte, _ uint64, _ uint32) ([]string, error) {
            return []string{"pk0", "pk1", "pk2", "pk3", "pk4"}, nil // consensus size 5 -> need 4
        },
    }
    verifyCalled := false
    args.MultiSigVerifier = &cMock.BelNevMock{
        CreateMock: func(pubKeys []string, index uint16) (crypto.MultiSigner, error) {
            return &cMock.BelNevMock{
                VerifyMock: func(msg []byte, bitmap []byte) error {
                    verifyCalled = true          // verifier is reached even though only 1 real signer bit is set
                    require.Equal(t, []byte{0xe1}, bitmap)
                    return nil                  // single-signer aggregate verifies OK
                },
            }, nil
        },
    }
    hdrSigVerifier, _ := headerCheck.NewHeaderSigVerifier(args)
    header := &block.Block{
        Header:        &block.BlockHeader{PrevRandSeed: []byte("seed")},
        PubKeysBitmap: []byte{0xe1}, // bit0 (real) + padding bits 5,6,7 => counted as 4/5 quorum
        Signature:     []byte("aggregate-of-only-real-bit-0"),
    }
    err := hdrSigVerifier.VerifySignature(header)
    require.NoError(t, err)   // <-- accepted with 1 real signature instead of the required 4
    require.True(t, verifyCalled)
}

Run: go test ./core/process/headerCheck -run TestPOCHeaderSigVerifierCountsPaddingBitsTowardQuorum -count=1 → ok. The test asserts the current code accepts the header; a corrected implementation must return an error because only one real signer bit is set.

Impact

This is an improper-verification / consensus-integrity vulnerability. A block proposer who can produce a valid leader signature plus a single valid aggregate BLS signature share can still satisfy the block-level quorum check by populating the padding bits of PubKeysBitmap. This weakens the PBFT two-thirds assumption: blocks can be accepted with fewer honest validator signatures than the protocol requires, enabling acceptance of attacker-favored blocks under collusion/compromise below the intended threshold and undermining finality guarantees. Any node that imports/intercepts headers (interceptedBlock.CheckValidity) is affected. Note the attacker still needs at least one valid consensus-group signature share and a valid leader signature, hence PR:L / AC:H.

Suggested fix

In verifyConsensusSize, count only bits whose index < consensusSize and additionally reject any non-zero bit in the padding region of the final bitmap byte (i.e. mask the last byte with (1 << (consensusSize % 8)) - 1 before counting, and fail if the original last byte has bits set above that mask). Mirror the same padding-bit rejection in blsMultiSigner.Verify so the verifier fails closed rather than silently ignoring unknown bits.

References

  • https://github.com/klever-io/klever-go/security/advisories/GHSA-f9h7-4mmq-vgcq
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-58262
  • https://github.com/klever-io/klever-go/commit/a11cb28e495e608d8034dbe83a91e89d0c68e0f7
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f9h7-4mmq-vgcq

items.content_html:
Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports leafnode connections between servers and message tracing through NATS headers.

Problem Description

Message trace destination checks were applied to ordinary client connections but not consistently to messages arriving through leafnode connections.

A leafnode operator could cause trace events to be sent to subjects that would not otherwise be permitted and could use trace-only behavior to prevent normal delivery or storage of affected messages.

Trace events can include routing, subscription, account, service import and JetStream metadata. The payload of the original application message is not chosen through the trace event itself.

Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.7 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.8.

Workarounds

Where possible, avoid granting publish paths from less-trusted leaf nodes into subjects for which trace-only behavior would affect delivery guarantees. No other known workarounds are available aside from upgrading to a fixed release.

References

  • GHSA advisory: https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-p3j5-5hrq-p75h
  • Credit: Koda Reef

items.content_html:
Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after failing to sufficiently restrict the set of configuration options defined in an .lfsconfig file in the repository.

Git LFS permits a limited set of configuration options to be defined in an .lfsconfig file at the root of a Git repository, but does not filter these options correctly if their keys contain certain additional components, which allows an attacker to mimic options that configure Git LFS to use a custom command to transfer objects. An attacker can then provide an arbitrary command which Git LFS will invoke when fetching objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by correctly restricting the configuration of custom object transfer commands to local Git configuration files.

Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 1.3.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

Workarounds

No single workaround exists other than to disable Git LFS entirely. As far as possible, users and administrators should avoid cloning repositories from untrusted sources.

For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

  • For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS discussion forum.
  • For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS security reporting policy.

items.content_html:
Impact

When fetching objects from a malicious repository, Git LFS may execute an arbitrary command or binary after incorrectly parsing the Git configuration options defined for a submodule.

Git LFS reads Git configuration options without checking for embedded line-ending control characters. By inserting control characters such as line feed (LF) into certain values, an attacker may be able to mimic options that cause Git LFS to execute an arbitrary command when fetching or adding objects.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by always using an unambiguous format to read and parse Git configuration options.

Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.6.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

Workarounds

To work around the problem, users should prevent Git from initializing any submodules by disabling the fetch.recurseSubmodules and submodule.recurse configuration options and by never running the git submodule init command. Any submodules which have already been initialized in a repository may be deactivated with the git submodule deinit command.

For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

  • For general questions, start a discussion in the Git LFS discussion forum.
  • For reports of additional vulnerabilities, please follow the Git LFS security reporting policy.

items.content_html:
Summary

Route selection uses the raw un-normalized request path, and the per-route ACL and basic-auth gates hang off that selection, so a dot-segment, encoded-dot, or double-slash variant of a protected path selects a different route, skips both gates, and is forwarded to the backend which normalizes and serves the protected resource. Unauthenticated; complete bypass of the access control the operator configured. Confirmed at HEAD b841544. Direct peers: Traefik CVE-2023-47106, Envoy CVE-2019-9901.

The defect

fabio never normalizes the request path. A repository-wide search for path.Clean returns zero results. Route selection uses the raw path (route/table.go line 487: if target = t.lookup(h, req.URL.Path, pick, match); target != nil {). Both access-control gates are properties of the target that lookup returned:

// proxy/http_proxy.go
if t.AccessDeniedHTTP(r) {                      // line 111, per-route allow / deny:ip ACL
    http.Error(w, "access denied", http.StatusForbidden)
    return
}
if !t.Authorized(r, w, p.AuthSchemes) {          // line 116, per-route auth= basic auth
    http.Error(w, "authorization failed", http.StatusUnauthorized)
    return
}

and the same raw path is forwarded verbatim (Path: r.URL.Path at line 142). So /./admin/, /%2e/admin/, //admin/ and /x/../admin/ do not match the protected /admin route. They fall through to the catch-all / route, which carries no ACL and no auth, and fabio forwards the un-normalized path to the origin, which normalizes it and serves the protected resource.

Verification

Verified end to end against the real binary at HEAD, not a synthetic unit test. fabio was built and run with static routes against a python3 -m http.server origin, driven with curl --path-as-is: on a basic-auth route, /admin/ returned 401 without credentials and 200 with valid credentials (controls correct), while all four crafted paths returned 200 with the protected page and NO credentials; on an ACL route, /admin/ returned 403 and all four crafted variants returned 200.

Precondition, stated honestly: a less restrictive route must reach the same backend so the crafted path has somewhere to fall through to. That is exactly the two-tag urlprefix- shape fabio's own access-control documentation instructs operators to configure. Where no fallback route exists the request 404s instead.

Suggested fix

Normalize the path before route lookup: decode percent-encoded dot segments and apply path.Clean, then match. Whether the normalized or original path is forwarded upstream is a separate decision, but the LOOKUP must run on the normalized form, because the ACL and auth decisions are derived from it. Also lowercase and strip the port and any trailing dot from the request host before host matching. Secondary observations: X-Forwarded-Prefix is passed through from the client on non-strip routes; the gRPC proxy path never calls either authorization gate, so allow=/auth= on a proto=grpc route are silently unenforced.

Dedup note

The obvious residual of CVE-2025-48865 is already taken: CVE-2026-62987 / GHSA-fq95-v8xc-jm3v (published 2026-07-03) covers the Connection-header strip of proxy.header.clientip/tls/requestid, fixed in v1.7.2. Do not re-report that. The finding above is a different and independent defect.

Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The bypass was reproduced against the real fabio binary with a live backend, including the 401-vs-200 and 403-vs-200 controls, and the reporter separately confirmed at HEAD that lookup takes req.URL.Path, that both gates derive from the returned target, that the raw path is forwarded, and that path.Clean appears nowhere in the repository.

The reporter manually verified this finding against the project's source at the location cited above before reporting it; the AI assistance noted above was for the audit and the drafting.

items.content_html:
Impact

After receiving an HTTP redirection, Git LFS may forward certain HTTP headers to a host other than the one for which they were intended. While Authorization headers are never forwarded to inappropriate hosts, Cookie headers may be forwarded incorrectly.

Git LFS has resolved this issue by never forwarding Cookie headers to hosts other than the ones for which they were intended. In particular, after an HTTP redirection is received to a URL with a different scheme, host, or port than found in the URL of the current request, any Authorization and Cookie headers from the current request will not be sent in the redirected request.

Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.5.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

Workarounds

No single workaround exists. As far as possible, users and administrators should review their systems to confirm no unnecessary HTTP redirections are performed, and that HTTP headers other than Authorization do not contain privileged or confidential information.

For more information

items.content_html:
Impact

When Git LFS makes object transfer or authentication requests to a remote host via SSH, it passes the path component of the remote's SSH URL as part of a command to be executed, but does not properly format the URL's path component as a single argument. By inserting shell meta-characters into the SSH URL, an attacker may be able to execute arbitrary commands on the remote host, if the host passes the commands to a shell without sanitizing them first.

Git LFS has resolved this problem by fully quoting the arguments of the remote commands it sends via SSH.

As well, Git LFS has resolved a problem with the default HTTPS URLs used when an SSH URL is configured for a remote host and the host either does not support Git LFS remote commands sent via SSH or supports HTTP authentication via SSH for Git LFS but does not return an explicit HTTP URL in response to a git-lfs-authenticate remote command. In these cases, Git LFS now correctly encodes the HTTPS URL used to contact the remote host.

Patches

This problem exists in all versions since 0.5.0 and is patched in v3.8.1. All users should upgrade to v3.8.1.

Workarounds

Users may set the lfs.sshTransfer Git configuration option to never, after which Git LFS will not attempt any object transfers over SSH. However, Git LFS will still make authentication requests to SSH URLs, so administrators of Git LFS services should ensure their systems sanitize all commands received over SSH before executing them.

items.content_html:
The defect

Confirmed at HEAD. server.go: cmdXCLIENT = []byte("XCLIENT") is 7 bytes (line 78), so the dispatch match cmdXCLIENT.match(cmd) only guarantees len(input) >= 7. The handler then slices input[8:] (line 586):

case sc.XClientOn && cmdXCLIENT.match(cmd):
    if toks := bytes.Split(input[8:], []byte{' '}); len(toks) > 0 {   // line 586

A client sending the bare command XCLIENT (exactly 7 bytes) hits input[8:7] and panics runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8:7]. handleClient runs in the per-connection goroutine (server.go:391) which has no recover(); the only recover() calls are in the backend mail-processing workers (a different goroutine never reached during command parsing), so the unrecovered panic crashes the whole SMTP daemon.

Input and attacker

Connect to the SMTP port, then send XCLIENT\r\n (a bare LF also works; no HELO needed). Precondition: xclient_on: true (off by default, but a documented nginx-fronted deployment; go-guerrilla does not restrict who may send XCLIENT). Attacker model: any unauthenticated client on the SMTP port.

Verification level

EXECUTED with a negative control (agent-run, driving the real server.handleClient with XClientOn=true over the suite's mock net.Conn). The bare XCLIENT panics with the exact OOB; the negative control XCLIENT with a trailing space (8 bytes) does not panic and returns 250. The upstream TestXClient tests XCLIENT ADDR=... and XCLIENT c but never the bare 7-byte form (the missing regression case). I independently re-confirmed at HEAD that cmdXCLIENT is 7 bytes (server.go:78), that the handler slices input[8:] (server.go:586), and that handleClient (server.go:391) has no recover. NOT verified: did not stand up a standalone daemon on a real socket to observe OS-level process exit (used the mock net.Conn plus the traced absence of recover; crash-to-exit is standard Go runtime behavior).

Suggested fix

Guard the slice against the exact-verb-length case: require len(input) > len(cmdXCLIENT)+1 (or slice at the verb length and trim) before input[8:]. A recover in the per-connection handleClient loop would also contain any residual command-parse panic to the single connection.

Also checked and SOUND

The rfc5321 recursive-descent parser (MAIL/RCPT/HELO/EHLO/address) is bounds-safe (next()/peek() return 0 at EOF), and the line/size/recipient caps are enforced. XCLIENT is the only off-by-one; every other command arm slices exactly at its verb length.

Advisory-source note

Five-source enumeration (repo advisories, OSV, NVD, the global GitHub DB, no vendor CNA) shows the PROXY-header IP-spoof bug (CVE-2025-31135, fixed v1.6.7) is the only published advisory; this XCLIENT panic is undisclosed and not contested.

Dedup

Dedup gate clean: no phires/go-guerrilla blocking verdict in COVERED-INDEX, DISCLOSURE-INDEX or SCOUT-EXCLUDE.

Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with a negative control (a bare XCLIENT crashes the real handleClient while XCLIENT with a trailing space returns 250), and the reporter confirmed at HEAD that cmdXCLIENT is 7 bytes while the handler slices input[8:] on a per-connection goroutine with no recover.

References

  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115578
  • https://github.com/phires/go-guerrilla/commit/b6deed97ff70f52bf34c386d33967694e7330d33
  • https://github.com/phires/go-guerrilla/commit/f0d0f2c40dcacf212e3a6a055ae67f7b412affc4
  • https://github.com/phires/go-guerrilla/releases/tag/v1.6.7-1

items.content_html:
What the fix did and the gap

The v2.3.0 fix (commit e88dabb) routed the _select field through a strict new gate, sanitizeSelectField (postgres.go:947/1003/2097). The sibling groupby path was left on the far weaker isSafeSQLExpression. adapters/postgres/postgres.go, GroupByClause (line 1946): a groupby field that contains balanced parens takes the raw-SQL-expression branch (around lines 1999-2006), gated only by isSafeSQLExpression (line 2001, defined at 2043). That gate validates only the OUTERMOST function name against a 13-entry allowlist and uses a character allowlist that permits spaces, single quotes and parens. It blocks ;, --, /* , unbalanced parens and an outer pg prefix, but NOT a trailing UNION SELECT ..., a nested (SELECT ...) subquery, or an inner pg function. sanitizeSelectField (the CVE fix) rejects exactly those.

Input and attacker

GET /{database}/{schema}/{table}?_select=id&_groupby=upper((SELECT+1))+UNION+SELECT+current_user. Sink trace: controllers/crud.go:131 calls GroupByClause unconditionally, concatenates it into sqlSelect (crud.go:133), executed at crud.go:176 with only the WHERE values parameterized. Reached after only a table read-permission check, passable unauthenticated in the default config (the same pipeline and attacker model as the anchor).

Verification level

EXECUTED with negative controls (agent-run go test ./adapters/postgres/, PASS): isSafeSQLExpression wrongly accepts four payloads and GroupByClause emits them raw (e.g. GROUP BY upper((SELECT 1)) UNION SELECT current_user, and GROUP BY abs((SELECT 1 FROM pg_sleep(3)))); negative controls with ; and -- are rejected; and sanitizeSelectField (the CVE fix) rejects the exact UNION payload the sibling gate accepts. I independently re-confirmed at HEAD that _groupby is gated by isSafeSQLExpression (postgres.go:2001) while _select uses sanitizeSelectField (postgres.go:947). NOT verified: end-to-end UNION exfiltration against a live Postgres (needs column/type alignment, Postgres-gated). The pg_sleep DoS primitive is unconditional and needs no alignment; char-by-char blind extraction is constrained (commas are pre-split, and =/</> are blocked).

Suggested fix

Route _groupby through the same strict gate as select (sanitizeSelectField-style: reject nested subqueries, UNION, inner pg functions, and anything past a single allowlisted function call), or parameterize/whitelist the group-by columns.

Also checked and SOUND

The other builders (WhereByRequest, OrderByRequest, JoinByRequest, CountByRequest, the jsonb/tsquery paths, ->>having, ident.IsValid) are sound; only the _groupby non-having function branch is the weak sibling.

Advisory-source note

Five-source enumeration: CVE-2025-58450 (GHSA-p46v-f2x8-qp98, "Systemic SQL Injection", GO-2025-3941) and the newer GHSA-qvx3-q8vx-9q3c (which covers _select, fixed v2.3.0). Neither mentions _groupby / GROUP BY. The systemic advisory's own "nested queries can be performed" note supports the incomplete-fix framing. Not contested.

Dedup

Dedup gate clean: no prest/prest blocking verdict in COVERED-INDEX, DISCLOSURE-INDEX or SCOUT-EXCLUDE.

Tooling

AI assistance wsa used while investigating. The injection is executed-verified with negative controls (isSafeSQLExpression accepts four UNION/subquery/pg_sleep payloads that GroupByClause emits raw, while ;/-- are rejected and the _select gate rejects the same UNION payload), and I confirmed at HEAD that _groupby uses the weak isSafeSQLExpression while _select was hardened with sanitizeSelectField.

items.content_html:
A server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw was found in KubeVirt's virt-api port-forward handler. When processing a port-forward request to a VirtualMachineInstance (VMI), virt-api reads the target IP from vmi.Status.Interfaces[0].IP and passes it directly to net.Dial() without validation. For VMIs using non-masquerade network bindings (bridge or secondary-only), this IP is reported by the QEMU guest agent running inside the VM and is fully controllable by the VM owner. An attacker with kubevirt.io:edit permissions can create a VM with a modified guest agent that reports an arbitrary IP address, then request port-forward to establish a bidirectional TCP tunnel from virt-api's cluster-internal network position to any routable destination, bypassing NetworkPolicy isolation.
